title: One defensible order
statement: An ordering item needs one defensible order: use only elements with a definite place, such as dated events or discrete steps, never a gradual process or ongoing condition.
detail: The ordering rubric classifies every element, and one whose starting event, law or publication can't be named is an ongoing state that caps orderability at 3 (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sequence_evaluation.txt`). Elements with explicit years or centuries turn the task into reading dates, and the stem must make the ordering criterion explicit, with no element referring forward in a way that reveals its position (the same file).
against: Dates are fine when the date is itself the curriculum fact being tested (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sequence_evaluation.txt`, lines 178-179). The same rubric judges an order against what is taught at the grade, and tells the judge to "accept it as correct (score 4 or 5) even if scholarly debate exists at a higher level" (`icloud-work/incept/inceptbench/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sequence_evaluation.txt`, line 97), so one definite place means one place at that grade.

evidence.quote: The test: if you cannot name the specific event/law/publication that STARTED this condition → it is an ongoing_state → orderability ≤ 3.
**Dates-in-items flag:** Items containing explicit years/centuries inline (e.g., "in 1492", "c. 1440 CE", "during the 15th century") reduce the task to date-reading rather than content knowledge.
Does the question stem make the ordering criterion explicit? Do items avoid forward references that reveal their relative position?
> "Can I name the specific moment this STARTED — a named law, event, publication, battle, or decree?"
- An item is classified ongoing_state or process → orderability ≤ 3 (regardless of position)
- BIOLOGY (5): "Arrange the stages of mitosis: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase" — each step has a unique, unambiguous position.
- ELA (1): "Arrange these themes from least to most important" — subjective, no correct order.
accept it as correct (score 4 or 5) even if scholarly debate exists at a higher level.
